questions.q: The editorial advises using every event as a “point of reference.” What does this mean?
options: Asking advice before every decision
Not quite. The article says: Turning each experience into an occasion to remember God and pray – for instance, a hurt into a prayer to be spared hurt in the eternal life.
Keeping a written record of each day
Not quite. The article says: Turning each experience into an occasion to remember God and pray – for instance, a hurt into a prayer to be spared hurt in the eternal life.
Turning each experience into an occasion to remember God and pray – for instance, a hurt into a prayer to be spared hurt in the eternal life
Yes. In this way one receives divine blessings every moment.
Comparing one’s life with that of others
Not quite. The article says: Turning each experience into an occasion to remember God and pray – for instance, a hurt into a prayer to be spared hurt in the eternal life.
questions.rationale: “When you undergo a hurtful experience in life, you can make it a point of reference and pray to God to save you from the hurtful experience of eternal life.”

questions.q: In what way does the editorial liken the mind to a mobile phone?
options: It works best when connected to others
Not quite. The article says: It must be recharged again and again, by constant reflection, to stay aware of God.
It can hold only a limited amount
Not quite. The article says: It must be recharged again and again, by constant reflection, to stay aware of God.
It should be switched off at night
Not quite. The article says: It must be recharged again and again, by constant reflection, to stay aware of God.
It must be recharged again and again, by constant reflection, to stay aware of God
Right. Otherwise distraction takes over.
questions.rationale: “A mobile phone becomes inactive when its battery gets exhausted and so we need to recharge it. The same is also true for our mind.”

questions.q: Muslims stand united in congregational prayer, yet often lack unity outside the mosque. How does the article explain this?
options: Unity in ritual meets no differences; real unity means staying together in spite of differences
Exactly. That needs conscious tolerance.
People forget prayer once they leave
Not quite. The article says: Unity in ritual meets no differences; real unity means staying together in spite of differences.
Prayer is led by one imam; society has many leaders
Not quite. The article says: Unity in ritual meets no differences; real unity means staying together in spite of differences.
Unity is possible only in small groups
Not quite. The article says: Unity in ritual meets no differences; real unity means staying together in spite of differences.
questions.rationale: “Real unity can only be established when differences are tolerated. Remaining united despite differences is the formula for true unity.”

questions.q: Every event appears to have a natural cause. What, says the article, is the test this sets for man?
options: To see the hand of God behind the cause, which is only a veil
Yes. This discovery is what the article calls faith.
To find a cause for every event
Not quite. The article says: To see the hand of God behind the cause, which is only a veil.
To control events through science
Not quite. The article says: To see the hand of God behind the cause, which is only a veil.
To deny that causes exist
Not quite. The article says: To see the hand of God behind the cause, which is only a veil.
questions.rationale: “Man needs to develop his consciousness so that he can see the hand of God behind every causal event. He should discover that in these events the cause is just a veil and not the reality.”

questions.q: A successful tailor said he had reached his position “by climbing a ladder and not by coming up to it in a lift.” What did he mean?
options: Progress comes step by step through long learning and hard work; there is no button to press
Correct. The article applies this to nation-building too.
He had refused all help from others
Not quite. The article says: Progress comes step by step through long learning and hard work; there is no button to press.
He distrusted modern machines
Not quite. The article says: Progress comes step by step through long learning and hard work; there is no button to press.
He had begun life in a tall building
Not quite. The article says: Progress comes step by step through long learning and hard work; there is no button to press.
questions.rationale: “There are no buttons which you can just push and automatically reach your goals. You can only make progress step by step.”

questions.q: An Eskimo who described New York to his village was named “the Liar.” What comparison does the article make?
options: The prophets, who told of an unseen world, were likewise called madmen and liars
Well read. People could not picture what they had never seen.
City life corrupts those who visit it
Not quite. The article says: The prophets, who told of an unseen world, were likewise called madmen and liars.
Travellers always exaggerate
Not quite. The article says: The prophets, who told of an unseen world, were likewise called madmen and liars.
Simple people are easily deceived
Not quite. The article says: The prophets, who told of an unseen world, were likewise called madmen and liars.
questions.rationale: “Just as the Eskimo was made to see a hitherto unknown world, so God gave the prophets a glimpse of the world that lies beyond death… people dubbed them madmen and liars.”

questions.q: The article says a community can feel abased while having numbers and resources. What causes this feeling?
options: Real poverty hidden by statistics
Not quite. The article says: False pride in a superior status and past glory, which makes whatever it has seem too little.
Unfair treatment by other nations
Not quite. The article says: False pride in a superior status and past glory, which makes whatever it has seem too little.
A lack of able leaders
Not quite. The article says: False pride in a superior status and past glory, which makes whatever it has seem too little.
False pride in a superior status and past glory, which makes whatever it has seem too little
Yes. The condition is psychological, not actual.
questions.rationale: “Muslims consider whatever they have got, to be less than what they imagine they should have, because of their false pride.”

questions.q: Why does the article call the discovery of one’s own helplessness “the greatest discovery”?
options: It turns a person to God in the kind of prayer that is sure to be answered
Right. All power is with God, all need with man.
It frees him from having to work
Not quite. The article says: It turns a person to God in the kind of prayer that is sure to be answered.
It shows that life has no purpose
Not quite. The article says: It turns a person to God in the kind of prayer that is sure to be answered.
It teaches him to depend on other people
Not quite. The article says: It turns a person to God in the kind of prayer that is sure to be answered.
questions.rationale: “This discovery gives him great prospects for remembering and beseeching his Lord… God’s mercy reaches him in return faster than the speed of light.”

questions.q: What does the article name as the “forbidden tree” of this world?
options: Travel
Not quite. The article says: Violence.
Wealth
Not quite. The article says: Violence.
Argument
Not quite. The article says: Violence.
Violence
Yes. To kill one person is like killing all mankind (Quran 5:32).
questions.rationale: “There is also a forbidden tree in this world and that is violence.” Habil’s words are given as the model: “Even if you raise your hand to kill me, I will not raise my hand to kill you.”

questions.q: The article speaks of “passive violence.” What is it, and how does it rank beside active violence?
options: Watching violence without helping – no fault
Not quite. The article says: Regarding others as oppressors and hating them – a sin of the same magnitude.
Refusing to defend oneself – a lesser fault
Not quite. The article says: Regarding others as oppressors and hating them – a sin of the same magnitude.
Regarding others as oppressors and hating them – a sin of the same magnitude
Well read. The difference is only outward.
Speaking harshly – a virtue when deserved
Not quite. The article says: Regarding others as oppressors and hating them – a sin of the same magnitude.
questions.rationale: “Passive violence is that wherein you regard others as oppressors and then show hatred towards them… Both these types of violence are sins of the same magnitude.”
